item.title: More than 200,000 join Amsterdam march against Gaza genocide
item.description:
More than 200,000 join Amsterdam march against Gaza genocide

Submitted by MEE staff on Mon, 11/09/2026 - 14:35
Protesters want the Netherlands to halt arms sales to Israel, tighten sanctions and recognise the Gaza genocide
Demonstrators take part in a "Red Line" protest demanding "government action to stop the genocide in Gaza" in Amsterdam on October 5, 2025. (Koen van Weel/ANP/AFP)
Off

Tens of thousands of people marched through Amsterdam on Sunday, demanding that the Dutch government end arms sales to Israel and impose tougher trade sanctions over its genocide in Gaza.

Many wore red for the Red Line protest, which drew more than 200,000 people, according to Amnesty International’s Dutch branch, one of the organisers.

Campaigners called on the Netherlands to formally recognise Israel’s actions in Gaza as genocide and denounced Israeli apartheid in the occupied West Bank.

Crowds chanted “Free, free Palestine!”.

“What is happening there is inhumane,” marcher Mike van Dongen told The Associated Press. “As far as I’m concerned, they are doing nothing,” he said. “They don’t dare take any serious steps.”

Palestinian medical authorities put the death toll in Gaza at 74,643, with 175,962 wounded.

The dead include about 22,000 children, and thousands of people remain missing beneath the rubble.

Since the 11 October 2025 ceasefire, 1,613 Palestinians have been killed in Gaza and 5,833 wounded. Israel’s war on Lebanon has killed more than 4,000 people since March.

Nearly 80 percent of Britons see Israel as a threat to world peace
Read More »

The International Criminal Court has issued arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over war crimes and crimes against humanity in Gaza.

In May, Middle East Eye reported that ICC prosecutors had applied under seal for a warrant to arrest Israeli Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich over war crimes and crimes against humanity against Palestinians in the occupied West Bank.

The Gaza genocide has strained Dutch ties with Israel. Caspar Veldkamp resigned as foreign minister last year after failing to win cabinet backing for further sanctions. The new minority coalition banned imports from illegal Israeli settlements in September. Israel responded by revoking the accreditation of Dutch diplomats.

Prime Minister Rob Jetten joined a Red Line march last year but skipped Sunday’s protest. At his weekly news conference on Friday, he defended his government’s response.

“Every single day and every single week, we do what we can to alleviate the terrible situation there,” he said. He added that his administration is “exerting greater political and diplomatic pressure” on Israel to abide by its agreements on Gaza.

item.title: Iran war: Will Trump's midterm defeat end or entrench the conflict with Tehran?
item.description:
Iran war: Will Trump's midterm defeat end or entrench the conflict with Tehran?

Submitted by Seyed Hossein Mousavian on Fri, 11/06/2026 - 16:29
The greatest victory for both nations would be neither military triumph nor the humiliation of the other, but the achievement of a lasting peace
An Iranian demonstrator holds a flag denouncing US President Donald Trump, in Tehran on 4 November 2026 (Atta Kenare/AFP)
Off

The US midterm elections delivered a historic defeat to President Donald Trump’s Republican Party, which lost control of both houses of Congress. 

Democrats achieved remarkable victories in traditionally Republican strongholds, including Texas and Kansas, while Abdul El-Sayed became the first Muslim elected to the US Senate. American newspapers described the outcome as a “blue tsunami” and a political demolition of Trump.

In Tehran, the election results were interpreted as a major political setback for the Trump administration, and a vindication of Iran’s resistance to US-Israeli military pressure. Iran’s top security chief, Mohsen Rezaei, wrote on X (formerly Twitter): “The Iranian nation handed Trump a strategic defeat on the battlefield and in the Hormuz - and a POLITICAL DEFEAT in Washington.” 

Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf appeared to share US Vice President JD Vance’s concerns about the political costs of the Iran war and the Republicans’ electoral defeat. 

Responding to Vance on X, Ghalibaf warned: “Boss is prepping the next war phase while America teeters on an Israel-First cliff. Skip the TED talk. Why not say this to your boss?” His message highlighted the possibility of common ground on ending the war.

Interestingly, the grievances identified by Vance closely resemble warnings that Iranian officials, international political figures, and I myself repeatedly raised in articles and interviews following the US-Israeli wars against Iran in 2025 and 2026. 

We warned that military confrontation would deepen regional instability, disrupt global energy markets, increase economic pressures on ordinary Americans, undermine Trump’s promise to avoid new wars, and further entangle Washington in Israel’s regional conflicts. Unfortunately, these warnings found little reception in Washington.

Opportunities and dangers

Yet the election does not automatically make a diplomatic breakthrough more likely. It creates both opportunities and serious dangers.

With both major American parties increasingly focused on the 2028 presidential election, Iran is likely to remain a central issue in their political confrontation, as it was during the midterms. Against this backdrop, Trump and the Republican Party face two fundamentally different choices.

The first is to transform the narrative of electoral defeat into one of military victory. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has openly advocated overthrowing Iran’s government, declaring that “there is only one way to remove this threat once and for all: overthrow the regime in Iran”. He also claimed that Trump had assured him the US was “ready to finish the job”. 

The message to US leaders, particularly Republicans, is increasingly clear: enough is enough. Americans do not want another endless war

Under pressure from such hawkish demands, Trump could be drawn into launching another massive offensive against Iran, hoping to achieve the regime change that previous military operations failed to deliver.

But this option rests on a dangerous assumption: that greater military force will succeed where the wars of 2025 and 2026 failed. Another major offensive could trigger devastating Iranian retaliation, threaten energy supplies, destabilise Washington’s regional allies, and prolong the conflict into the 2028 election. 

Rather than rescuing the Republicans, it could produce an even greater political disaster. If Trump chooses renewed military escalation, figures such as Defence Secretary Pete Hegseth would likely play leading roles in its implementation.

The second option is to transform the electoral setback into a historic diplomatic opportunity through an “Islamabad plus” framework built on two complementary pillars: the memorandum of understanding brokered by Pakistan earlier this year, and new regional security arrangements. 

The first step would be to revive and expand the Islamabad memorandum to end the war and resolve outstanding disputes, including Iran’s nuclear programme, freedom of navigation through the Strait of Hormuz, the lifting of the US maritime blockade, and other critical security and economic issues.

The “plus” would establish an inclusive regional security and cooperation framework, building on the mediation efforts of regional actors - Pakistan, Turkey, Saudi Arabia, Egypt, Qatar and Oman - to promote collective security, economic cooperation and sustainable peace. 

Qatar’s foreign minister, Sheikh Mohammed bin Abdulrahman Al Thani, has said that Gulf countries and Iran need a framework based on cooperation, sovereignty and mutual security. Oman’s foreign minister, Badr al-Busaidi, has called on the Arab Gulf states, Iraq and Iran to unite under a single “non-aggression” security pact.

Such an agreement could stabilise energy markets, ease inflationary pressures, protect regional countries from further destruction, and create more favourable conditions for addressing the Israeli-Palestinian conflict.

Trump could thus secure a historic legacy: ending decades of US-Iran hostility and helping to establish a new regional security architecture, rather than pursuing another devastating war. If Trump chooses this path, Vance should lead the diplomatic initiative.

Overriding priorities

The debate in Tehran is equally consequential. One school of thought favours continuing the confrontation until the US suffers a decisive strategic defeat, withdraws its military forces from the region, and abandons Netanyahu’s “Greater Israel” project.

Some proponents of this approach also advocate withdrawing from the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT) and developing nuclear weapons. They argue that decades of NPT membership, Iran’s religious prohibition against nuclear weapons, and extensive cooperation with the International Atomic Energy Agency failed to prevent sanctions, sabotage, and ultimately military attacks. 

Trump's midterm defeat gives the Gulf a chance to escape America's forever wars
Read More »

Ebrahim Rezaei, a member of the National Security and Foreign Policy Committee, said 10 proposals to withdraw from the treaty had been registered, and withdrawal was under consideration, according to the Fars news agency. According to this view, nuclear deterrence offers stronger protection than international legal commitments. 

According to what I have heard from individuals close to key decision-makers in Tehran, Iran still prefers a negotiated settlement.

However, repeated US military attacks despite diplomatic efforts, particularly the collapse of the Islamabad MOU, have deepened scepticism about Vance’s peace initiative.

In the absence of an agreement, Tehran appears determined to respond to any renewed US attack by expanding the confrontation into a full-scale regional war, targeting US military infrastructure across the region, and fundamentally reshaping regional security arrangements to prevent future attacks by Washington and Tel Aviv.

Signalling its preparedness for a potentially wider war, Iran’s IRGC has announced the removal of its self-imposed 2,000-kilometre ballistic missile range limit, maintained for nearly three decades. This follows Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei’s warning that Iran’s response to future US or Israeli attacks would have no geographical limits.

But this strategy carries enormous risks. A prolonged war of attrition would devastate Iran’s economy, increase human suffering, endanger neighbouring countries, and threaten global stability. Pursuing nuclear weapons could also invite further attacks before Iran could establish a credible deterrent. 

A settlement based on humiliation, coercion or one-sided concessions would merely prepare the ground for another conflict

Iran’s overriding national priorities should be securing a permanent end to the war, and overcoming its severe economic challenges. Prolonged confrontation would accomplish neither.

The alternative is a comprehensive diplomatic settlement that protects Iran’s sovereignty, legitimate security interests, and economic future. 

For negotiations to succeed, however, Washington and Tehran must recognise one fundamental principle: any sustainable agreement must be honourable and mutually beneficial. Neither will accept unconditional surrender. A settlement based on humiliation, coercion or one-sided concessions would merely prepare the ground for another conflict. 

That is why a Vance-Ghalibaf diplomatic initiative, built around an “Islamabad plus” framework and supported by key regional powers, deserves serious consideration.

History offers a powerful lesson: from the political backlash against the Vietnam War in the 1970s, to the Republicans’ electoral defeats amid the Iraq War in 2006, and the Iran war two decades later, prolonged military confrontations have repeatedly imposed heavy political costs on Washington. 

The message to US leaders, particularly Republicans, is increasingly clear: enough is enough. Americans do not want another endless war. Military superiority does not guarantee strategic victory. 

Trump and Tehran now face a historic choice between further confrontation and a diplomatic settlement. The greatest victory for both nations would be neither military triumph nor the humiliation of the other, but a lasting peace that ends decades of hostility and establishes a new era of regional security and cooperation.

The views expressed in this article belong to the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial policy of Middle East Eye.

item.title: Nearly 80 percent of Britons see Israel as a threat to world peace
item.description:
Nearly 80 percent of Britons see Israel as a threat to world peace

Submitted by Elis Gjevori on Mon, 11/09/2026 - 13:01
Israel’s genocide in Gaza and the war on Iran have driven a sharp shift in British public opinion
Pro-Palestinian supporters hold placards and wave flags in central London, on 11 October 2025 (Henry Nicholls/AFP)
Off

Nearly four in five Britons see Israel as a serious threat to world peace, according to a survey published last week by the National Centre for Social Research (NatCen).

The figure rose from 48 percent in 2005 to 78 percent this spring, two-and-a-half years into the genocide in Gaza and just after Israel and the US had attacked Iran.

In July, a YouGov opinion poll commissioned by the Council for British-Arab Understanding found that only 17 percent of the British population believes that Israel is not committing genocide in Gaza.

The war on Iran has hit the UK economy, leaving households paying more for energy, food and mortgages. The rising bills have brought the cost of Israel’s wars in the Middle East home to British households.

Last week, the Bank of England raised its base rate from 3.75 percent to 4 percent, its first increase in more than three years. The rise pushes up payments for borrowers on mortgages and adds to the cost of taking out or renewing a home loan.

Before the war with Iran started, economists had expected rates to fall.

British attitudes towards Israel have shifted sharply over the past three years. By autumn 2024, a year into Israel’s genocide in Gaza, 73 percent of Britons saw Israel as a serious threat to world peace.

Israel has killed at least 74,643 Palestinians in Gaza, including more than 22,000 children, and wounded 175,962. Around 10,000 more are missing and most are presumed dead under the rubble.

Since the so-called ceasefire on 11 October last year, Israel has killed 1,613 Palestinians in Gaza and wounded more than 5,833 people. More than 4,000 Lebanese were killed in Israel's offensive against Hezbollah earlier this year.

British views of the US have also soured. Some 74 percent of Britons now regard the US as a serious threat to world peace.

NatCen, the largest social research institute in the UK, found that “following the bitter public disputes with Nato allies over Greenland, and the decision in February 2026 to, alongside Israel, embark on a bombing campaign in Iran, the proportion of Britons who saw the United States as a threat to global peace rose again, to 74 percent.”

UK government facing legal challenge over IHRA antisemitism definition in schools
Read More »

In 1994, under President Bill Clinton, 22 percent of Britons saw the US as a serious threat. By 2005, two years after President George W Bush led the illegal invasion of Iraq, that figure had risen to 47 percent.

“However, that a clear majority of the population have come to regard Britain’s most important ally in the post-war international order as a threat to global peace is undoubtedly novel,” the report said.

The findings come from the annual British Social Attitudes survey, the UK’s longest-running survey of social and political attitudes. NatCen has conducted it since 1983.

The survey found that 89 percent of Britons see Russia as a serious threat to world peace, compared with 62 percent who say the same of China. 

Around 75 percent of Britons view Iran as a threat, up from 67 percent in the spring of last year.

The report said that “the country has moved psychologically from a post-Cold War society at peace, to one that has come to accept permanent geopolitical competition as the new strategic reality”.

That shift comes amid an ongoing war in Europe, Israeli threats to the Middle East, growing competition between the West and China, and an increasingly belligerent US.

item.title: Iranian press review: Newspapers warn of war reaching 'heart of Europe'
item.description:
Iranian press review: Newspapers warn of war reaching 'heart of Europe'

Submitted by MEE correspondent on Mon, 11/09/2026 - 11:02
Meanwhile, a report says Republican losses in Congress will not stop Trump's military campaign, a former Israeli negotiator says Israel sought to fragment Iran and China emerges as a potential player in efforts to end the war
The Hamshahri daily published a map of Europe on its front page on 3 November 2026, marking US bases in the UK, Germany, France, Italy, Romania, Greece, Albania and Portugal as the 'target bank of the Iranian armed forces' (screengrab)
Off

IRGC-linked outlets publish list of potential targets in Europe

Daily newspapers close to Iran’s Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) have published a list of potential targets across Europe, following US strikes on Qeshm Island last week.

The reports came as speculation grows over a possible return of the US to the war with Iran.

On Tuesday, the Hamshahri daily published a map of Europe on its front page, marking US-used bases in the UK, Germany, France, Italy, Romania, Greece, Albania and Portugal as the “target bank of the Iranian armed forces”.

Hamshahri described Iran’s new military strategy as one “of confrontation without geographical limits”, borrowing a term the country's Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei previously used.

Under this strategy, the daily wrote, “US support centres, air and naval bases, and logistical infrastructure in Europe have been raised as potential targets”.

The Kayhan daily, whose editor is appointed by the supreme leader, also issued a warning. It said that if the US did not accept Iran’s conditions for a peace deal, “the geography of the battle will expand to the heart of Europe and the depth of overseas bases”.

It added that Iran’s military doctrine towards the US, Israel and their allies had become “more direct and more offensive”.

Among European countries involved in the war against Iran, Kayhan singled out the UK, saying it had played “the most key and prominent role”.

Could Iraq's 2006 experience be repeated in Iran in 2026?

As senior Iranian officials welcomed the Republican Party's defeat in the US midterm elections as a blow to President Donald Trump's hawkish policies, the news website Khabar Online drew comparisons with the 2006 midterms, held during the US-led occupation of Iraq.

In its report, Khabar Online warned that “a change in the congressional majority and opposition to war policies do not necessarily mean an immediate retreat by the president or an end to military operations”.

'Iron Gate plan is merely wordplay': Iran mocks US military initiative to disrupt supply routes
Read More »

The report recalled the Republican Party's similar defeat under the then president George W Bush and examined its impact on the war in Iraq, including the extensive powers the US president used to continue military operations.

It also looked at US military operations in Iraq after 2006, when Washington increased the number of troops on the ground.

“The expectation of some opponents of the war was that a Democratic victory would pave the way for a rapid withdrawal of US forces from Iraq. But what happened in the following months was the opposite,” the report said.

Drawing on the comparison, Khabar Online concluded: “The Bush experience shows that even an anti-war majority in Congress cannot, on its own, stop the government's military course without political unity and the ability to overcome a presidential veto.”

Israel sought to break up Iran, former Israeli negotiator says

Daniel Levy, an Israeli peace negotiator who took part in the 1993 Oslo-B talks, said Israel's reasons for launching a new war against Iran on 28 February were to break it up and follow a policy similar to what happened in Iraq and Syria.

“Israel's goal was the collapse of the state, the creation of chaos in Iran and the break-up of the country - something similar to what we saw in Iraq and Syria,” he said in an interview with BBC Persian.

He added: “I don't think the Israelis themselves even believed their own propaganda narrative that regime change could be achieved in Iran.”

Leak reportedly exposed Netanyahu and Mossad chief's plan to attack Iran before Israeli election
Read More »

On the plan to divide Iran, Levy also pointed to reports in the early days of the war about weapons being sent to Iranian Kurdish opposition groups in Iraq.

He said the initial idea was to establish a liberated area inside Iran, where resources and military forces could be concentrated to continue the war against the central government.

Levy also referred to Reza Pahlavi, the son of Iran's deposed shah, who had received public support from Tel Aviv since Israel's 2025 attack on Iran. He described Israel's backing of Pahlavi as a temporary strategy aimed at advancing its longer-term goals.

“The Pahlavi family was a useful tool for Israel. A tool for creating chaos. I don't believe they thought the end result would be regime change. I don't even think they considered that a desirable outcome,” he said.

Tehran looks to Beijing as war diplomacy intensifies

Speculation is growing over China's possible role in efforts to secure a ceasefire between Iran and the US, as diplomatic contacts between Tehran, Beijing and Muscat point to a possible new channel for negotiations.

The pro-reformist Shargh daily reported that security official Ali Bagheri Kani's recent meetings in Beijing could signal the creation of “a parallel diplomatic path” led by China and Oman.

Shargh added: “Bagheri Kani's visit, within this framework, could be part of Tehran's consultations to assess new diplomatic initiatives and explore the capacity of influential countries to prevent the crisis from escalating.”

Meanwhile, the conservative Jame Jam daily also covered Bagheri Kani's visit, describing it as part of Iran's efforts to bring Beijing and Moscow on board with its regional policies.

According to Jame Jam, Tehran's diplomatic efforts and consultations with China and Russia, alongside the use of mediators such as Qatar and Pakistan, are part of Iran's attempt to manage the war it has faced since February.

However, the daily stressed that statements of support from China and Russia alone could not prevent the conflict from continuing. It said the effectiveness of their policies depended on practical action to prevent US unilateralism in the region.
